questions.question_text: Which one of these random variables is continuous?

options.text: The volume of petrol, in litres, pumped into a car
The number of goals scored in a football match
options.why: Goals are counted, so the values go up in separate whole-number steps.

options.text: The number of eggs in a carton
options.why: Eggs are counted, so only whole-number values are possible.

options.text: The shoe size chosen from the sizes a shop stocks
options.why: The sizes stocked form a listed set of separate values, so the variable is discrete.

questions.solution_text:
Petrol volume is measured, so it can take any value in an interval.
The other three are counts or a listed set of sizes.
The volume of petrol is the continuous variable.

questions.question_text: The temperature at noon is recorded to the nearest whole degree Celsius. Which statement about the temperature is correct?

options.text: It is continuous, because temperature can take any value in an interval even though the record is rounded
It is discrete, because the recorded values are whole numbers
options.why: Treats the rounding of the record as if it were the values the quantity itself can take.

options.text: It is discrete, because only finitely many temperatures occur during the year
options.why: Counts the recorded outcomes rather than asking whether the quantity is measured.

options.text: It is continuous, because more than $30$ different values are possible
options.why: Confuses having many possible values with filling a whole interval.

questions.solution_text:
Temperature is measured, so the true value can be anywhere in an interval.
Rounding changes how the value is written, not the quantity itself.
The variable is continuous.

questions.question_text: $T$ is the continuous time, in seconds, that a randomly chosen car waits at a set of lights. Find $P(T = 15)$.

options.why: Treats the $15$ possible whole seconds as equally likely outcomes of a discrete variable.
Reads the total probability of the whole distribution as the probability of one value.

options.text: It cannot be found without the density $f(t)$
options.why: Assumes a single value has a positive probability that the density would reveal.

questions.solution_text:
$T$ is continuous, so the region above a single value has zero width.
$P(T = 15) = 0$

questions.question_text: A continuous random variable $X$ has $P(X < 14) = 0.62$. Find $P(X \le 14)$.

options.why: Treats $X \le 14$ as the complement of $X < 14$ and subtracts from $1$.
Halves the probability, as though the endpoint splits it between the two inequalities.
Assumes the single value $14$ carries a positive probability that must be added on.
Adds the two cumulative probabilities instead of subtracting them.
Computes $1 - 0.79$, which is the probability above $13$ rather than the interval.
Computes $1 - 0.24$, which is the probability above $6$ rather than the interval.

questions.question_text: A continuous random variable $X$ has $P(X \le 5) = 0.31$ and $P(X \ge 9) = 0.26$. Find $P(5 < X < 9)$.

options.why: Subtracts the two given probabilities instead of removing both tails from $1$.
Removes only the lower tail, forgetting the probability above $9$.
Removes only the upper tail, forgetting the probability below $5$.

options.text: $P(2 < X < 7)$ is less than $0.58$, because the two endpoints are removed
options.why: Assumes each endpoint carries a positive slice of probability.

options.text: $P(2 < X < 7) = 0.42$, since $P(X = 2)$ and $P(X = 7)$ must be taken from $1$
options.why: Takes the complement instead of recognising that the endpoints contribute nothing.

options.text: $P(2 < X < 7)$ cannot be found without the density $f(x)$
options.why: Assumes the endpoint probabilities must be computed from the density rather than being $0$.

questions.solution_text:
$P(X = 2) = P(X = 7) = 0$ because $X$ is continuous.
$P(2 < X < 7) = P(2 \le X \le 7)$
$= 0.58$

questions.question_text: $H$ is the continuous height, in centimetres, of a randomly chosen adult. Why is $P(H = 172) = 0$?

options.text: A single value has no width, so the area under the density curve above it is $0$
Because no adult is ever exactly $172$ cm tall
options.why: Claims the outcome is impossible, when it is possible but of zero probability.

options.text: Because the density curve has height $f(172)=0$ at that value
options.why: Reads the height of the density curve as the probability of the value itself; the density at $172$ is not $0$, yet the probability of that single height still is.

options.text: Because heights are always rounded to the nearest centimetre
options.why: Blames the rounding of the record rather than the zero width of a single point.

questions.solution_text:
Probability for a continuous variable is area under the density curve.
The value $172$ is a single point, so the strip above it has zero width and zero area.
$P(H = 172) = 0$
